attempts.jsonl.key_identity: Coupling exists iff the transportation polytope {mu >= 0 : marginals P_{H_1}, P_{H_2}, P_H on disjoint unions} is nonempty; nonempty in all 1360+ tested instances.
attempts.jsonl.method: Exact linear-programming feasibility of the coupling on random and structured instances.
attempts.jsonl.obstruction: No general construction; the naive conditional splitting fails.
attempts.jsonl.result: Since |X_1| = dim H_1, |X_2| = dim H_2 and |X_1 union X_2| = dim H almost surely, any such coupling has X_1 and X_2 disjoint a.s.; the question is therefore the feasibility of the transportation polytope with marginals P_{H_1}, P_{H_2} and the disjoint-union marginal P_H. I solved this LP exactly (HiGHS, minimum total constraint violation) on 1360 random pairs of orthogonal subspaces of l^2(E) with |E| in {3,...,6} and all dimension splits, on generic instances with |E| = 7, 8, on Fourier-mode subspaces on cycles of length 5..8, and on star-space splits in the edge space of K_4 (uniform spanning tree kernels): every instance was feasible with zero violation (raw/C_lyons_q28_lp_check.json, raw/C_lyons_q28_lp_check_structured.json). This extends the numerical support the source mentions. A structural observation: the feasibility is equivalent to the existence of a Markov kernel from P_H to pairs, i.e. a random rule splitting a P_H-sample C into (C_1, C_2) with the right marginals; for H = l^2(E) the rule is trivial. I looked for a canonical rule (sample X_1 from P_{H_1} conditioned on X_1 subset of C, then X_2 = C minus X_1) and checked on |E| = 4 that this canonical rule does NOT give the correct marginal for X_2 in general, so the coupling, when it exists, is not the naive conditional one.

attempts.jsonl.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.jsonl.method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov.
attempts.jsonl.obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.
attempts.jsonl.result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part.

attempts.jsonl.key_identity: The 2x1-rectangle 6-cycles exist in Z^d but not in the hypercube; their normalised count is one order in 1/d below the three-direction 6-cycles, predicting the first discrepancy at a_4.
attempts.jsonl.method: Compare the short cycle structure of Z^d and the hypercube to predict the first differing coefficient.
attempts.jsonl.obstruction: Not proved; requires the fourth-order lace diagrams on both graphs.
attempts.jsonl.result: The coefficients a_i are determined by the counts of closed non-backtracking walks of length up to 2i in the graph (the lace-expansion diagrams at order i involve random-walk loops of length up to 2i, up to the normalisation by (2d)^i). Z^d and the hypercube both have degree 2d (resp. d, with the appropriate rescaling) and both have girth 4; the number of 4-cycles through a vertex is d(d-1)/2 ... for Z^d: choose two distinct directions, 4 sign patterns give (2d)(2d-2)/2 cycles; for the hypercube choose two coordinates: d(d-1)/2 cycles; after the normalisation by degree these agree to leading order, which is why a_2 agrees. 6-cycles: in Z^d a 6-cycle uses three directions (counts (2d)(2d-2)(2d-4)/...), or two directions with a back-and-forth (which is backtracking-free? a 6-cycle in two directions like ++-+-- exists in Z^2: no, in Z^2 6-cycles do not exist since the square lattice is bipartite with girth 4 and 6-cycles would need ... Z^2 has cycles of length 6? A closed walk of length 6 that is a simple cycle in Z^2 encloses 2 squares: yes, the 2x1 rectangle has perimeter 6. In the hypercube a simple 6-cycle uses exactly three coordinates (a 6-cycle in Q_3 exists); in Z^d a 6-cycle can use two directions (the 2x1 rectangle) or three. The hypercube has no 2x1 rectangle analogue (in Q_d, two coordinates span a 4-cycle only). So the 6-cycle counts differ at relative order 1/d^2: Z^d has extra 6-cycles using only two directions, of number of order d^2 versus the three-direction ones of order d^3; the 1/d^2-relative difference in the 6-cycle count enters the coefficient at order (2d)^{-3} x (1/d^2)... The source says a_3 agrees, consistent with the two-direction 6-cycles being of lower order; they enter at order 1/d beyond a_3's leading diagrams, i.e. at a_4 or a_5. Prediction: the first differing coefficient is a_4 (from the 2x1-rectangle 6-cycles, absent in the hypercube), unless their contribution cancels, in which case a_5. This is a heuristic prediction, not a proof; the source's hint that the proofs in [173, 174] suggest a difference at some i >= 4 is consistent.

attempts.jsonl.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.jsonl.key_identity: Oriented paths cannot return to earlier times, so the zigzag overcount should be replaceable by a backbone-branching flow with convergence for d > 4.
attempts.jsonl.method: Identify which estimate needs d > 6 and whether it is an artefact.
attempts.jsonl.obstruction: The improved flow construction is not carried out.
attempts.jsonl.result: The source's proof of the Alexander-Orbach behaviour for the oriented IIC uses a zigzag-path count converging like sum_m m^{(4-d)/2}, which needs d > 6, while the oriented IIC's mean-field structure (Hofstad-den Hollander-Slade) holds for d > 4. The zigzag count controls the resistance between the origin and level n via the number of paths that go up, come back down and go up again; in d = 5, 6 these counts diverge, meaning the crude flow bound fails, but the true resistance may still be of order n (mean-field, tree-like) because the divergent terms are overcounting: paths in the oriented IIC cannot return to earlier times, so a zigzag in the bound corresponds to two disjoint upward paths connected through the IIC's backbone, whose number is controlled by the two-point function squared, giving a convergent sum for d > 4 if the backbone is used correctly. So I expect the Alexander-Orbach value d_s = 4/3 to hold for the oriented IIC in d = 5, 6 as well, and the obstruction to be technical (the resistance lower bound of Kumagai-Misumi type needs a better flow construction using the backbone). This is a prediction with a proposed route (flow along the oriented backbone with branching at the pivotal levels), not a proof.

attempts.jsonl.independent_check: Both results are widely cited; not re-fetched in this session.
attempts.jsonl.key_identity: Random d-regular max independent density 2 log d/d vs factor-of-iid bound log d/d (Rahman-Virag): the conjectured equality fails at the maximum.
attempts.jsonl.method: Compare the two sets on what is known: the maximum independent set density versus the best factor-of-iid density.
attempts.jsonl.obstruction: none for the refutation; the residual question is trivial by dilution
attempts.jsonl.result: One inclusion is a theorem: any factor-of-i.i.d. independent set on the tree can be transferred to random d-regular graphs (large girth) with the same density up to o(1), so factor densities are achievable. The conjecture is the converse: every achievable density is a factor density. It is known to FAIL at the maximum: for large d the maximum independent set density of random d-regular graphs is 2 log d/d (1+o(1)) (Ding-Sly-Sun for large d) while factor-of-i.i.d. independent sets have density at most log d/d (1+o(1)) (Rahman-Virag 2017), a factor of 2 gap. Hence the conjecture as stated in the source is false for the maximal density, at least for large d; the surviving question is the characterisation of the achievable set below the factor threshold (which is an interval [0, alpha_factor] by dilution, already covered) versus the interval [0, alpha_max] of achievable densities. Recorded as refuted at the top density by Rahman-Virag together with Ding-Sly-Sun (bounded recall of both).
